headline: Falkner Island Porgies Won't Quit, Blues Sneaking Back Into the Gulf
subhead: The rockpiles are stacked with porgies and keeper sea bass while the first real bluefish push in weeks starts nosing into Milford Gulf and the New Haven breakwalls.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, second drift off the outer New Haven breakwall, my nephew Nico's ultralight nearly went swimming before I got the net under it — a fat porgy, thick through the shoulders, that hit a piece of green crab like it hadn't eaten in a week. That's been the story on the rockpiles all week: porgies stacked deep, feeding hard, and not particularly picky about how you present it to them.

I've been running the same milk run I run every August — Falkner Island's south side rockpile, the Charles Island bar, and the riprap along both breakwalls at New Haven Harbor — and the porgy bite has been the one constant while everything else sorts itself out. Anchor up in 15 to 25 feet on the down-current side of the structure, two-hook bottom rigs, size 4 or 2 hooks, green crab or sandworm, just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. On the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming at Falkner, we've been putting eight, ten fish in the cooler an hour without much effort — mixed in with keeper sea bass to 16 inches that clearly haven't gotten the memo that summer's supposed to be slow for them.

Sea bass have actually been the pleasant surprise this week. Stratford Shoal, on the western edge where the rockpile drops into 30-35 feet, has been holding fish that don't feel like they've been picked over yet — probably because most of the boat traffic out there is running past toward the bass grounds and not stopping to jig. Bucktail teasers tipped with squid strips, dropped right to bottom and worked with short hops, have been the ticket. Bring green crab too — on the slower bites, a live crab on a plain hook out-produces the jig two to one.

Blackfish are still finding their legs. Season's open and I'm seeing a few caught almost by accident by guys targeting porgy and sea bass on the same rockpiles — crushed green crab worked slow along the base of the structure at Charles Island has turned a couple of decent tog in the 16-18 inch range. It's not a dedicated bite yet, more of a bonus, but as the water starts easing off its summer high I expect that to sharpen up through September.

Striped bass are the harder conversation right now. Surface water's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s across the Central Sound, which is pushing most of the real feeding activity down onto structure and current lines rather than up top where you can see it. The Charles Island sandbar has still been giving up fish on the tide change — not a blitz, but a legitimate bite — working live-lined bunker or a bucktail with a chunk of pork rind or Gulp trailer, right where the bar drops off into the channel on the last two hours of the flood. We flagged this pattern last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon should sharpen things up at current-driven structure — and that's exactly what's playing out. The moon's set for the 12th, and I've noticed the current already running harder through the Charles Island rip and around the Milford Gulf breakwater than it was ten days ago. That extra push is going to matter.

Bluefish are the story I've been waiting to write. After a genuinely quiet July out here, there's a real resurgence building from the western end of the Sound and it's starting to nose into our water. I had a report of a mixed bag off the Milford Gulf breakwall Thursday evening — a couple of two- and three-pound blues mixed in with the porgies, hitting small metal jigs meant for something else entirely. That's usually the tell. When blues start showing as bycatch on bottom rigs, it means the schools are pushing bait up shallow and it's only a matter of days before they're actively working the surface. I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a half-ounce Kastmaster or a small diamond jig on deck at the New Haven breakwalls and Hammonasset this week, just in case that surface bite flips on. Worth noting — if you're fighting stripers anywhere near structure loaded with bluefish activity, don't dawdle on the release. No shark issue out here like they've got out east, but a longer fight in warm water does the fish no favors either way.

Fluke have been the disappointment of the summer, honestly. I'm not going to sell you a story that isn't there — the sand flats off Hammonasset and the mouth of the Housatonic near Milford Gulf have been giving up mostly short fish, a keeper here and there on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid, drifted slow on the last of the ebb. If fluke's your priority this week, I'd treat it as a bonus while you're anchored up working the rockpiles for porgy, not a dedicated mission.

Looking ahead: if that tidal push keeps building into the 12th like it's been building the last few days, I expect the Charles Island bar to turn on harder for stripers on the flood, and I wouldn't be shocked if the bluefish push solidifies into something you can plan a trip around by this weekend. Best case, we get a real surface bite at the breakwalls before the week's out. If the blues stall out west of us, I'd just keep doing what's working — porgies and sea bass on the rockpiles, blackfish as the bonus, and a rod rigged for blues just in case.
